Where it began

Kerry James O'Keeffe was born on 25 November 1949 in Hurstville and went to Marist College Kogarah. He bowled leg breaks, and his first-class career began in 1968–69, when he was 19. The next season brought him 35 first-class wickets and a tour of New Zealand, where he picked up 22 more.

When England came to Australia in 1970–71 he took 6 for 69 and made 55 not out for New South Wales against them. That was enough for the selectors, and he made his Test debut in the fifth Test of that Ashes series.

The player

Recalled for the seventh Test at Sydney, on a pitch that suited spin, he took 3 for 48 and 3 for 96. He spent 1971 with Somerset and took 77 wickets at 23.57 in English conditions. Back in the Test side, he played all five Tests in the West Indies in 1973 and helped Australia to a narrow win in the third. Against New Zealand in 1973–74 he made 85 and took six wickets in a big Australian win.

His best Test figures, 5 for 101, came on a later tour of New Zealand. Soon after he played in the Centenary Test, opening the batting in the second innings and taking 3 for 108, including Derek Randall and Tony Greig, as Australia won. In 24 Tests from 1971 to 1977 he took 53 wickets at 38.08 and made 644 runs at 25.76, with a best of 85.

What made him special

He was a spinner who could bat as well, good enough to be sent in to open in the Centenary Test. He did not quite become the next great Australian leg-spinner, as some had hoped, but he gave plenty of good days.

He was always the first to poke fun at his own bowling. He liked to point out that 44 of his 53 Test wickets were caught, a higher share than any other Test bowler's in his telling, as proof that he rarely beat the bat. A favourite story was of an umpire turning down his appeal for leg before because the ball had turned too much. O'Keeffe took it as a gentle dig at how little he spun it.

Away from the middle

After playing he found a second calling behind the microphone, first on ABC Radio. Listeners loved his after-dinner style of storytelling, his rich Australian phrases and his unmistakable laugh. He took particular delight in puzzling the Indian broadcaster Harsha Bhogle with them. Underneath the fun there was real insight, built on his own career and a deep knowledge of the game's history and figures.

In 2004 he published an autobiography, According to Skull. He stepped away from commentary in January 2014, came back with Triple M in December 2016 and joined Fox Sports from the 2018–19 season. He was on air for them in the 2025–26 season.

And finally

Most bowlers keep quiet about their averages. O'Keeffe turned his into decades of entertainment. Few bowlers have got more laughs out of 53 wickets, or shared them so generously.
